query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The catalytic performance of a transition‐metal catalyst is governed by the oxidation state of its surface sites; specifically, a higher degree of controlled surface oxidation enhances selectivity by finely tuning the adsorption energies of reactants.
generation.material_initial_state: A pristine transition‐metal catalyst (e.g., platinum or palladium) with its native surface oxide/hydride layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled modification of the surface oxidation state through pretreatment: one set of catalysts is exposed to an oxidative atmosphere while another set is exposed to a reductive (or inert) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Mild thermal treatment (around 150–200°C) for a fixed duration (e.g., 1 hour) under controlled atmospheres (oxygen-rich for oxidation or hydrogen/inert for reduction) prior to performing the catalytic reaction under standard reaction conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The surface oxidation state of the metal atoms, which influences the d-band electron density and, consequently, the adsorption energies of key reactants.
generation.mechanism: Controlled oxidation of the surface sites alters the binding strengths of adsorbed species. An oxidized surface modifies the adsorption energy so as to favor reaction pathways that yield more selective outcomes (e.g., partial oxidation products) rather than complete oxidation or side reactions, thereby also affecting durability by limiting over-adsorption and subsequent deactivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts pretreated in an oxidative atmosphere will have a higher fraction of oxidized surface sites, resulting in improved selectivity toward the desired products compared to those pretreated under reductive conditions. In contrast, the reductively pretreated catalysts may show higher conversion rates but at the cost of lower selectivity due to over-adsorption and side reactions.
generation.baseline: Catalysts with no deliberate pretreatment (i.e., possessing their native surface oxidation state).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under mild thermal and atmospheric conditions that do not induce significant sintering or structural phase changes. It is most applicable to reactions in which the adsorption energy modulation is a key determinant of reaction pathway, typically in selective oxidation or reduction reactions.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in activity, selectivity, and durability may vary with the specific transition metal, reaction system, and exact pretreatment parameters. The degree to which surface oxidation state influences performance in highly dynamic or extreme conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of identical catalysts: one group with no pretreatment (baseline), one pretreated under oxidative conditions, and one pretreated under reductive conditions. Characterize all catalysts using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to determine the surface oxidation state, then perform the catalytic reaction under identical reaction conditions for all groups while recording conversion, selectivity, and durability over time.
measurements: XPS for quantification of surface oxidation state
Long-term durability through repeated cycles or time-on-stream tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic correlation is observed between the pretreatment-induced surface oxidation state and the measured differences in catalytic selectivity (i.e., if oxidative pretreatment does not consistently lead to improved selectivity compared to reductive pretreatment or baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.
